findings.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The embedded-server client path swaps the previous 30-second local permission cache (old newRBACClient with cache.NewLocalCache) for authzlib.WithCacheClientOption(&NoopCache{}), which never stores or returns anything. Every authz Check/List call made through the in-process embedded client (the primary path for monolithic Grafana deployments) now goes straight to the authz server/store on every request instead of being served from cache for up to 30s — a per-request DB/service-call hot-path regression for all embedded users of this client.

[BUG] Negative results are cached in permDenialCache with only the generic shortCacheTTL and no invalidation hook, so a user who is denied once keeps being denied for up to the TTL after their permissions are granted. An admin grants a user access to a dashboard they were just denied on; the user's next Check calls hit the denial cache entry set at line 153 and return Allowed=false without consulting the store, so the user is locked out of the newly-granted resource for up to shortCacheTTL — no test in the diff covers grant-after-denial invalidation, and the existing permission invalidation code paths (which flush permCache) have no knowledge of the new perm_*_name_parent keys.

[ADVISORY] getCachedIdentityPermissions returns the cached map[string]bool by reference from the shared permCache and Check/List then hand that same map to checkPermission/listPermission while other goroutines concurrently receive the identical map from the cache. Any mutation of the permission map inside checkPermission/listPermission (e.g., decorating folder scopes) races with concurrent readers of the same cached entry across goroutines, producing a data race or corrupted shared cache state that surfaces as intermittent wrong allow/deny under load; the new tests exercise only single-threaded cache hits so this is unverified by the diff.

[BUG] The new permDenialCache is written on every deny (service.go line 153-155) but no invalidation path anywhere in this diff deletes userPermDenialCacheKey entries, so the existing permission-invalidation flow (which presumably clears userPermCacheKey/basicRoleCache keys when permissions change) leaves denial entries intact. A user whose access is denied once is served Allowed=false from the denial cache for up to shortCacheTTL after an administrator grants them the permission — the grant is invisible until the denial entry expires, breaking the authorization contract that permission changes take effect promptly.

[BUG] The denial cache hit path increments requestCount with cachedStatus "false" and returns immediately without consulting permCache or the store, but the denial key is built from checkReq.ParentFolder as supplied by the caller (service.go line 116), not from the resolved folder hierarchy that checkPermission uses. Two Check calls for the same dashboard — one with Folder set, one without — use different denial keys, so denial caching silently misses or, worse, denies based on a stale entry from a request that omitted the folder, while the actual folder-based permission decision would differ.

[BUG] When getCachedIdentityPermissions returns cached permissions but checkPermission evaluates allowed=false (line 134-137), the code falls through and refetches via getIdentityPermissions, yet the freshly computed denial is then cached (line 153-155) even though the cached permission snapshot may simply have been stale — the denial derived from a fresh fetch is correct, but the inverse case is not handled: a cached-perms allow short-circuits without ever confirming against fresh state while the permDenialCache entry from an earlier deny sits alongside it, and which one wins depends on insertion order within the same TTL window. Within one shortCacheTTL window, a Check for resource X that was denied (populating denial cache) followed by a permission grant produces: denial-cache hit denies, permCache (refreshed by getUserPermissions on grant-triggered invalidation elsewhere) allows — the stale denial wins, contradicting the permCache invalidation contract.

[ADVISORY] TestService_CacheCheck covers allow-from-cache, DB-fallback, outdated-cache-fallback, and a denial-cache hit, but contains no test for denial-cache behavior after permissions are granted (stale denial) and no test for the invalidation path of permDenialCache at all. The next change to invalidation logic (e.g., adding a Delete on permission change) has no regression test to anchor against, and the stale-denial failure mode above ships undetected; whoever modifies the denial cache TTL or invalidation will not be alerted by CI.

[ADVISORY] The 'outdated cache' subtest's comment claims the cache 'does not have the permission for dash2 (outdated)' but the test name and body actually exercise the intentional always-fall-through-on-deny design (cached perms exist, checkPermission denies, DB re-consulted) — the test never asserts that permCache was refreshed or that metrics reflect the fallback path. A future maintainer reading this test believes cache staleness is detected and handled, when actually the design is to refetch on every cached deny — masking the doubled DB cost per denied request and leaving the metrics claim (permissionCacheUsage 'false' then a second fetch) unverified.

[ADVISORY] userPermDenialCacheKey embeds userUID, action, name, and parent, making the denial cache a per-user-per-resource entry with unbounded cardinality, unlike the per-user-per-action permCache — for a high-traffic namespace with many denied resource checks this multiplies cache entries by the number of distinct (resource, folder) pairs per user. Operators running the in-process local cache (or a shared cache backend) see memory/Redis key growth proportional to denied-request cardinality within each TTL window; a bot or scanner enumerating resource names floods the cache with single-use denial entries.

[ADVISORY] getCachedIdentityPermissions handles TypeAnonymous by reading permCache, but no test in the diff exercises the cached path for anonymous or render-service identities through Check or List — the only new cache tests use TypeUser subjects. The TypeAnonymous branch's permCache key (anonymousPermCacheKey with ns+action) and the TypeRenderService ErrNotFound bypass are unverified; a regression in either branch (e.g., caching render-service permissions, or wrong anon key) would break anonymous dashboard viewing with no CI signal.

[BUG] The new permDenialCache entries are never invalidated by any existing permission-change invalidation path, because its key format (userPermDenialCacheKey adds name and parent suffixes) is disjoint from the userPermCacheKey-based keys that invalidation code deletes. When an admin grants a user permission on a resource, the existing cache-invalidation flow clears the perm cache but not the denial entry, so the user keeps receiving Allowed:false from Check for up to shortCacheTTL after the grant — a security-visible stale-deny window that the previous cache design (which only cached positive permission data and always fell back to a fresh checkPermission on the stale entry) did not have.

[BUG] When getCachedIdentityPermissions returns a cache hit but checkPermission evaluates allowed==false, Check unconditionally falls through to s.getIdentityPermissions and, on a confirmed deny, calls s.permDenialCache.Set — including for identity types where the cached perms may be legitimately incomplete (e.g. the TypeRenderService/default branches always miss, but the TypeUser branch caches only the scoped perm map that checkPermission already rejected), and the Set is performed with no namespace-scoped guard distinguishing 'denied because stale scoped cache' from 'denied in DB'. A user whose scoped permission map is cached-but-outdated (permission revoked or granted at DB level within TTL) gets a fresh denial entry written keyed on that outcome; combined with the missing invalidation path this doubles the stale-deny window and lets the denial cache pin results computed from two different data sources within one request.

[ADVISORY] Moving the permCache read out of getUserPermissions/getAnonymousPermissions into getCachedIdentityPermissions changes the semantics of the permissionCacheUsage metric: it now only fires on the Check/List call paths (with label 'false' also emitted when a cache hit exists but checkPermission denies), and never fires for getIdentityPermissions callers or the render-service path, whereas previously every getUserPermissions invocation labeled it. Operators with Grafana dashboards tracking authz cache hit-rate by action see label distributions shift after this deploy (hit-rate appears to drop for actions served via render-service or direct getIdentityPermissions calls), and the 'false' label now conflates 'cache miss' with 'cache hit but not allowed' in Check.

[ADVISORY] The diff deletes TestService_getUserPermissions' cache-hit case and adds no test exercising the permDenialCache expiry/grant-recovery behavior — i.e., the new behavior-bearing denial cache's interaction with permission changes and TTL is entirely untested. A regression in denial-cache eviction or in the invalidation gap (finding 1) would pass the full test suite and only surface as users reporting they cannot access newly granted resources in production.

[BUG] The permission-denial cache is populated (line ~153 `s.permDenialCache.Set(ctx, permDenialKey, true)`) but no invalidation path anywhere in this diff deletes denial entries when a user's permissions change, and the denial key format (`namespace + ".perm_" + userUID + "_" + action + "_" + name + "_" + parent`) diverges from the permCache key format (`namespace + ".perm_" + userUID + "_" + action`), so any existing invalidation that targets the permission cache key/prefix pattern does not necessarily match denial entries. A user who is granted access to a resource (e.g. added to a role or given dashboard permissions) keeps receiving Allowed=false for up to shortCacheTTL on every Check, even after the permission cache itself has been invalidated/refreshed — a stale-deny window longer than the permCache staleness, producing access denials that outlive the permission cache's invalidation guarantees.

[BUG] When the permission cache HIT yields a denial (allowed==false) and no denial entry exists, Check falls through to `s.metrics.permissionCacheUsage.WithLabelValues("false", checkReq.Action).Inc()` and refetches from the database, recording a cache miss for a request that was actually served from cache and issuing a full DB permission load on every such request. The permissionCacheUsage metric systematically under-reports hit rate for deny outcomes (any cached-perms deny with no prior denial entry is logged as "false" and triggers a redundant getIdentityPermissions DB round-trip), so dashboards monitoring cache effectiveness and DB load on the authz hot path show wrong numbers and the cache provides no benefit for first-time denies.

[ADVISORY] The denial-cache lookup and the permission-cache lookup are two parallel caches with overlapping but non-identical key grammars built by string concatenation (userPermCacheKey vs userPermDenialCacheKey in cache.go lines 27-32), where the denial key is the perm key plus `_name_parent` segments — a hand-maintained pair of formats with no shared constructor. The next editor who adds a cache key component (e.g. a folder-path discriminator or identity type) or who writes an invalidation that prefixes on the perm-key pattern will update one format and silently miss the other, producing either denial entries that never match (dead cache) or an invalidation that can't reach denial entries; denials also bypass the folder-tree logic entirely, so a resource moved between folders serves stale denials keyed to the old parent until TTL expiry.

[ADVISORY] In List, the cached permissions map returned by getCachedIdentityPermissions (the same map instance stored in the shared permCache) is passed directly to listPermission without any defensive copy, and the same shared-map-by-reference pattern now flows through two read paths (Check via checkPermission and List via listPermission). If listPermission (or any future consumer of the cached map) mutates the map — e.g. adding computed wildcards or normalizing scopes — it corrupts the cached entry for all subsequent requests in the TTL window, turning a shared cache into cross-request state contamination; the exposure is new because this diff adds a second consumer path to the raw cached value.

[BUG] The new permDenialCache has no invalidation path, so cached denials persist for shortCacheTTL after a user's permissions are granted, unlike the previous behavior where denials were re-derived from a permCache that existing invalidation code evicts on permission changes. An admin grants a user access to a dashboard they were just denied; the existing permission-change invalidation logic evicts userPermCacheKey entries but knows nothing about userPermDenialCacheKey, so the user keeps getting Allowed:false from the stale denial entry for up to shortCacheTTL, a silent authz-behavior regression relative to the pre-diff contract that invalidation preserved.

[BUG] The denial cache key embeds the request's ParentFolder value verbatim, so the same resource checked with Folder set versus unset produces two independent denial keys and the cached denial leaks into or fails to apply across the two access patterns inconsistently. A Check with ParentFolder="fold1" that is denied populates key ..._dash1_fold1; a subsequent identical request without Folder (ParentFolder="") gets a different key and skips the denial, and a denial recorded for the folder-less key also does not cover folder-inherited access — denial caching becomes path-dependent, which the original always-recomputed Check never was.

[ADVISORY] ProvideAuthZClient silently swaps the in-process authz client from a 30s local cache (newRBACClient) to authzlib.NewClient with NoopCache, removing client-side response caching with no flag or config escape hatch. Every in-process authz Check RPC that previously served from the 30s client cache now hits the server each time; operators relying on that cache to blunt burst load on the authz service cannot re-enable it without a code deploy, and the change was not surfaced as a documented behavioral trade-off in the diff.

[ADVISORY] Denial-cache hits are counted under the permissionCacheUsage metric with hit="true", conflating two distinct cache layers into one metric series. Anyone monitoring permissionCacheUsage hit-rate to tune the permission cache TTL will see inflated hit rates from denial entries whose misses never populate the metric path (the hit branch increments but the denial-cache miss is indistinguishable), so cache-tuning dashboards silently change meaning with this diff.

[BUG] The new permDenialCache is written on every deny (line ~153) but this diff adds no invalidation path for it, so denials survive permission-cache invalidation events. When a user's permissions change (role granted), existing invalidation logic purges the userPermCache entries, but denial entries keyed as namespace+".perm_"+userUID+"_"+action+"_"+name+"_"+parent (cache.go:30-32) are not registered with any Delete/invalidate call in this diff; a user who was denied once is denied again from the stale denial cache even after the grant, breaking authorization correctness — this is the authorization-cache-asymmetry pattern (grants get fresh DB re-lookup, cached denials are served without revalidation).

[ADVISORY] userPermDenialCacheKey embeds the raw request-supplied Name and ParentFolder, producing an unbounded per-resource key space that no exact-key invalidation can cover. Operators performing cache invalidation on permission change cannot enumerate the (action, name, parent) combinations previously denied for a user, so any invalidation strategy short of deleting by prefix will leave stale denial entries; whoever wires up invalidation next must know about this second key family or the deny cache silently diverges from the grant cache.

[BUG] A denied Check is written to permDenialCache with no invalidation in this diff, so a permission granted within shortCacheTTL is still denied, and the new TestService_CacheCheck only asserts the deny-on-hit path — it never tests a subsequent grant after a cached denial, leaving the stale-denial window completely unverified. A user who has a dashboard shared to them within ~30s of a denied Check keeps getting Allowed=false from the denial cache even though the permission store and permCache now say allowed; no test in the diff exercises grant-after-deny, so a regression or TTL increase here ships silently.

[ADVISORY] The new getCachedIdentityPermissions switch branches for types.TypeAnonymous (cache hit), types.TypeRenderService (always miss), and the default error path are exercised by no test in the diff — TestService_CacheCheck and TestService_CacheList only cover TypeUser via 'user:test-uid' subjects, and no other test file in the diff (only pkg/services/authz/rbac/service_test.go changed) calls Check or List with an anonymous or render-service subject. A regression in the anonymous cached-permission path (e.g. wrong cache key or returning stale perms) or the default-case error handling would not be caught by any test; anonymous traffic through the authz service is a major request path.

[ADVISORY] The new cached-branch error path in Check (checkPermission failing on cachedPerms) increments requestCount with the 'true' cache-usage label combination but the tests never trigger it, and no test asserts any metrics label values for the new denial/cached paths at all — the new tests assert only resp.Allowed. If the label wiring for the new cache paths is wrong (the deny path labels requestCount 'false' while permissionCacheUsage is 'true'), dashboards built on permissionCacheUsage will misreport hit rates, and no test will notice because metrics are never asserted in TestService_CacheCheck/CacheList.

[BUG] The new permDenialCache is written on every denied Check but has no invalidation path anywhere in this diff, so a permission grant does not clear previously cached denials. When an admin grants a user access to a dashboard (the permission-updated path invalidates permCache/idCache but never touches permDenialCache), the user keeps receiving Allowed:false from the denial entry for up to shortCacheTTL after the grant, breaking the previously-immediate effect of permission changes; the same staleness applies when a resource is moved into a folder the user can read.

[BUG] Check caches a denial (permDenialCache.Set) even when the deny decision was computed from a stale permCache hit path falling through to the database, and it stores the denial keyed on the raw request's Name/ParentFolder without ensuring ParentFolder was resolved. A request whose ParentFolder field is empty (or resolved later inside checkPermission against the folder tree) writes a denial under key suffix '_<empty>' that is never matched by later requests carrying an explicit folder, and vice versa, so denials are cached under inconsistent keys; more importantly, any transient deny (e.g., mid-deploy skew, folder tree still cold) is pinned for the full TTL with no way to purge it.

[BUG] On a permDenialCache hit, Check returns Allowed:false without ever validating that the subject's identifiers or permissions were loadable, so a deny caused by a transient backend error path that reached the Set at line ~153 is replayed as an authoritative deny. The Set at the bottom of Check runs unconditionally whenever !allowed, including denies that stem from degraded store reads surfaced through getIdentityPermissions' non-error deny results; users whose check was denied during a partial backend failure stay locked out of that exact resource for the full TTL with no re-evaluation, whereas pre-diff behavior re-queried the store on every request.

[BUG] The new permDenialCache is written on every DB-backed denial but has no invalidation path anywhere in the diff, so a cached denial survives permission grants. A user denied once is denied for the full shortCacheTTL (30s) even after an admin grants the permission and any permission-change invalidation fires — permCache gets invalidated on writes but permDenialCache is a new key family no existing invalidation code knows about, so the grant silently fails to take effect until TTL expiry; the denial-cache-hit branch returns Allowed:false without ever consulting fresh state.

[ADVISORY] A permDenialCache hit is recorded as permissionCacheUsage("true") and requestCount(cache_hit="true") even though the permission cache itself was never consulted, corrupting cache-hit dashboards. Operators tuning cache effectiveness see inflated permission-cache hit rates driven by denial entries, and cannot distinguish denial-cache hits from permission-cache hits when debugging authz latency/staleness; the metric content misdirects the investigation.

[ADVISORY] Non-ErrNotFound errors from getCachedIdentityPermissions (e.g. a store failure from GetUserIdentifiers for TypeUser) are silently discarded with no log and the code falls through to getIdentityPermissions, which re-issues the same identifier query. When the identifier store is failing, every Check pays a doubled, unlogged round trip to the failing store before the error is finally surfaced by getIdentityPermissions, and the transient failure is invisible in logs because only the final error is recorded.

[ADVISORY] When cached permissions are found but evaluate to allowed==false, permissionCacheUsage is incremented with "false" (cache miss) even though the cache was a hit, and the code then re-fetches from the store and overwrites the denial cache entry. Dashboards under-report permission-cache effectiveness because denies via cached data are counted as misses, and operators measuring cache benefit from these metrics get a systematically wrong picture of the Check fast path.

goldens.comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.
The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.

The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The embedded-server client path swaps the previous 30-second local permission cache (old newRBACClient with cache.NewLocalCache) for authzlib.WithCacheClientOption(&NoopCache{}), which never stores or returns anything. adjudication.rationale: The diff does show that the embedded/in-process client construction in `ProvideAuthZClient` is changed from `newRBACClient(channel, tracer)` to `authzlib.NewClient(..., authzlib.WithCacheClientOption(&NoopCache{}), ...)`, and the newly added `NoopCache` always returns `cache.ErrNotFound` and never stores anything. That verifiably removes the previous client-side 30s local cache behavior for the embedded path (while `newRemoteRBACClient` still uses `cache.NewLocalCache` with 30s expiry). However, the finding overstates the impact: `service.go` now adds server-side caching (`getCachedIdentityPermissions` and `permDenialCache` short-circuiting in `Check`/`List`), so embedded calls may still avoid DB/store hits even without a client cache. The real diff-grounded issue is a potential performance/architecture regression (extra RPC/server work, altered caching layer placement) rather than a clear functional bug or guaranteed per-request DB hit.

adjudication.rationale: In `Service.Check`, the new `permDenialCache` is consulted first (`if _, ok := s.permDenialCache.Get(...); ok { return Allowed: false }`), and a denial entry is set whenever the DB-backed check returns `!allowed` (`s.permDenialCache.Set(..., true)`). Unlike `permCache`, which only short-circuits on cached *allow* (and falls through to the store when cached perms don’t allow), a cached denial will force `Allowed=false` without consulting the store for up to `shortCacheTTL`. The diff shows no invalidation mechanism for these `userPermDenialCacheKey(...)` entries, so a grant-after-denial can be incorrectly denied until TTL expires.

adjudication.rationale: In this diff, getCachedIdentityPermissions returns the cached value from s.permCache directly (a map[string]bool). In Go, maps are reference types, so returning the cached map hands callers a reference to shared underlying state. Check() and List() now pass that map into s.checkPermission / s.listPermission on cache-hit paths. The diff does not show whether those functions (or anything they call) mutate the map, so the claimed race/corruption is not directly verifiable here; however, the change clearly increases the surface area for accidental mutation of a shared cached map, and the new tests only cover single-threaded cache-hit behavior without exercising concurrent access.

On any computed deny, the code unconditionally writes `s.permDenialCache.Set(ctx, permDenialKey, true)`. Unlike the positive-permission cache path, this denial short-circuit does not fall back to DB when the cached decision might be stale. The diff shows no deletion/invalidation of `userPermDenialCacheKey(...)` entries anywhere, so after permissions are granted, an existing denial entry can continue to force `Allowed=false` until TTL expiry.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows the denial cache key is built from `checkReq.ParentFolder` (`userPermDenialCacheKey(..., checkReq.ParentFolder)`) and the request returns immediately on a denial-cache hit. However, the finding’s core claim—that `checkPermission` uses a *resolved* folder hierarchy that can differ from the caller-supplied folder, making the denial key inconsistent with the actual permission decision—is not verifiable from the provided diff (the `checkPermission` logic and how `checkReq.ParentFolder` is derived are not shown). The added test (`Should deny on explicit cache deny entry`) also treats the folder as an explicit request parameter used for the key, which supports this being intended behavior. The statement about `requestCount` using a “cachedStatus” label value is also not grounded because the label semantics are not shown in the diff.

adjudication.rationale: In Service.Check(), the new permDenialCache is consulted first and immediately returns Allowed=false on a cache hit (service.go:113-121). Denials are cached after a fresh permission fetch when allowed==false (service.go:150-154), but there is no corresponding invalidation/clearing of permDenialCache when permissions later become allowed (and the allow fast-path from permCache returns early at service.go:124-137). Therefore, within shortCacheTTL, a previously cached denial for a specific (namespace,user,action,name,parentFolder) will override any later granted permissions and cause incorrect denies until TTL expires. The finding’s “insertion order” detail is off (denial cache always wins because it’s checked first), but the underlying stale-denial behavior is a real defect introduced by this diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] TestService_CacheCheck covers allow-from-cache, DB-fallback, outdated-cache-fallback, and a denial-cache hit, but contains no test for denial-cache behavior after permissions are granted (stale denial) and no test for the invalidation path of permDenialCache at all. The next change to invalidation logic (e.g., adding a Delete on permission change) has no regression test to anchor against, and the stale-denial failure mode above ships undetected; whoever modifies the denial cache TTL or invalidation will not be alerted by CI.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds new negative-caching logic via `permDenialCache` in `Service.Check`: it returns an immediate deny on `permDenialCache.Get(...)` hit (service.go `Check`, early return) and sets `permDenialCache` on any computed deny (`if !allowed { s.permDenialCache.Set(...) }`). The new tests in `TestService_CacheCheck` cover cache-allow, DB fallback, outdated-perm cache fallback, and an explicit denial-cache hit, but they do not cover the stale-denial scenario where a previously-set denial remains and wrongly overrides newly-granted permissions until TTL, nor do they cover any invalidation behavior (and the diff contains no `Delete`/invalidation logic for `permDenialCache`). This is a concrete gap in test coverage for the newly introduced denial cache behavior.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The 'outdated cache' subtest's comment claims the cache 'does not have the permission for dash2 (outdated)' but the test name and body actually exercise the intentional always-fall-through-on-deny design (cached perms exist, checkPermission denies, DB re-consulted) — the test never asserts that permCache was refreshed or that metrics reflect the fallback path. A future maintainer reading this test believes cache staleness is detected and handled, when actually the design is to refetch on every cached deny — masking the doubled DB cost per denied request and leaving the metrics claim (permissionCacheUsage 'false' then a second fetch) unverified.

adjudication.rationale: In `TestService_CacheCheck` the subtest "Fallback to the database on outdated cache" sets `permCache` to only allow `dash1` and then checks access to `dash2`, which causes `Service.Check` to (1) successfully load cached perms via `getCachedIdentityPermissions`, (2) get `allowed == false` from `checkPermission`, and then (3) always fall through to `getIdentityPermissions` (DB-backed) to re-evaluate and allow. The test only asserts the final `Allowed==true`; it does not assert that the cache was refreshed nor that metrics reflect the intended fallback path. This makes the name/comment about "outdated cache" potentially misleading because the observed behavior is simply "refetch on cached deny/miss", and the diff also shows `permissionCacheUsage` is incremented as "false" whenever cached perms exist but do not allow (since only the cached-allow early return increments "true").

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] userPermDenialCacheKey embeds userUID, action, name, and parent, making the denial cache a per-user-per-resource entry with unbounded cardinality, unlike the per-user-per-action permCache — for a high-traffic namespace with many denied resource checks this multiplies cache entries by the number of distinct (resource, folder) pairs per user. Operators running the in-process local cache (or a shared cache backend) see memory/Redis key growth proportional to denied-request cardinality within each TTL window; a bot or scanner enumerating resource names floods the cache with single-use denial entries.

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces a new `permDenialCache` keyed by `userPermDenialCacheKey(namespace, userUID, action, name, parent)` (added in `cache.go`) and used in `Service.Check` to short-circuit denies: it does `permDenialCache.Get(...)` early and `permDenialCache.Set(..., true)` whenever `!allowed` after the DB-backed check (`service.go`). Unlike `permCache`, which is keyed per-user-per-action (`userPermCacheKey(ns, uid, action)`), the denial cache is per-user-per-action-per-(name,parentFolder), which can create many distinct keys for denied probes within the TTL window. That is a concrete operational/scalability concern introduced by this change, but not a verifiable functional correctness defect from the diff alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] getCachedIdentityPermissions handles TypeAnonymous by reading permCache, but no test in the diff exercises the cached path for anonymous or render-service identities through Check or List — the only new cache tests use TypeUser subjects. The TypeAnonymous branch's permCache key (anonymousPermCacheKey with ns+action) and the TypeRenderService ErrNotFound bypass are unverified; a regression in either branch (e.g., caching render-service permissions, or wrong anon key) would break anonymous dashboard viewing with no CI signal.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds new branching logic in `getCachedIdentityPermissions` for `types.TypeAnonymous` (reads `permCache` using `anonymousPermCacheKey(ns.Value, action)`) and `types.TypeRenderService` (always returns `cache.ErrNotFound`). The new cache-focused tests (`TestService_CacheCheck`, `TestService_CacheList`) only exercise `Subject: "user:test-uid"` (TypeUser) paths; there is no new test that drives `Check`/`List` with an anonymous subject or a render-service identity to validate these branches/keys. This is a specific, diff-grounded testing gap rather than a demonstrated functional bug.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The new permDenialCache entries are never invalidated by any existing permission-change invalidation path, because its key format (userPermDenialCacheKey adds name and parent suffixes) is disjoint from the userPermCacheKey-based keys that invalidation code deletes. When an admin grants a user permission on a resource, the existing cache-invalidation flow clears the perm cache but not the denial entry, so the user keeps receiving Allowed:false from Check for up to shortCacheTTL after the grant — a security-visible stale-deny window that the previous cache design (which only cached positive permission data and always fell back to a fresh checkPermission on the stale entry) did not have.

adjudication.rationale: The diff clearly introduces a new negative-result cache (permDenialCache) that is consulted first in Check() and can force an immediate deny (service.go:113-141), and entries are added on deny (service.go:150-154) using a new key shape that includes name/parent (cache.go:30-32). The diff does not show any corresponding invalidation/deletion logic for these new keys; however, the finding’s claim about an “existing permission-change invalidation path” clearing only userPermCacheKey-based entries cannot be verified from the provided diff because no invalidation code is shown. What is verifiable is that this change creates a new cache namespace with a more specific key format and no visible integration into any invalidation mechanism in this diff, which is a concrete correctness-risk/maintenance concern.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] When getCachedIdentityPermissions returns a cache hit but checkPermission evaluates allowed==false, Check unconditionally falls through to s.getIdentityPermissions and, on a confirmed deny, calls s.permDenialCache.Set — including for identity types where the cached perms may be legitimately incomplete (e.g. the TypeRenderService/default branches always miss, but the TypeUser branch caches only the scoped perm map that checkPermission already rejected), and the Set is performed with no namespace-scoped guard distinguishing 'denied because stale scoped cache' from 'denied in DB'. A user whose scoped permission map is cached-but-outdated (permission revoked or granted at DB level within TTL) gets a fresh denial entry written keyed on that outcome; combined with the missing invalidation path this doubles the stale-deny window and lets the denial cache pin results computed from two different data sources within one request.

adjudication.rationale: In `Service.Check`, a cached-permissions hit that yields `allowed == false` does *not* write to `permDenialCache`. The code only calls `s.permDenialCache.Set(...)` after it falls back to `s.getIdentityPermissions(...)` and then computes `allowed` from the DB-backed `permissions` (lines added around `if !allowed { s.permDenialCache.Set(...) }`). Therefore the denial cache is populated only on a DB-confirmed deny, not on a deny derived from an incomplete/stale cached permission map. The finding’s core claim that results from two different data sources are pinned within one request via `permDenialCache.Set` is not supported by the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] Moving the permCache read out of getUserPermissions/getAnonymousPermissions into getCachedIdentityPermissions changes the semantics of the permissionCacheUsage metric: it now only fires on the Check/List call paths (with label 'false' also emitted when a cache hit exists but checkPermission denies), and never fires for getIdentityPermissions callers or the render-service path, whereas previously every getUserPermissions invocation labeled it. Operators with Grafana dashboards tracking authz cache hit-rate by action see label distributions shift after this deploy (hit-rate appears to drop for actions served via render-service or direct getIdentityPermissions calls), and the 'false' label now conflates 'cache miss' with 'cache hit but not allowed' in Check.

adjudication.rationale: The diff does change `permissionCacheUsage` metric emission semantics in a diff-verifiable way. The cache-read/metric logic was removed from `getUserPermissions` (deleted `s.permCache.Get` block and the associated `permissionCacheUsage` increments) and from `getAnonymousPermissions` (deleted cache get), and replaced with a new `getCachedIdentityPermissions` used only by `Check` and `List`. In `Check`, `permissionCacheUsage` is incremented with label `"true"` only when cached perms both exist and `checkPermission(...)` returns allowed; otherwise it increments `"false"` after that block, meaning `"false"` now covers both cache-miss and cache-hit-but-denied cases. Also, `getCachedIdentityPermissions` returns `cache.ErrNotFound` for `types.TypeRenderService`, so `Check`/`List` will always emit `"false"` for that path, and any other callers of `getIdentityPermissions` (outside `Check`/`List`) would no longer produce `permissionCacheUsage` signals at all. This is a real, specific operational/observability change, but not a functional correctness defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The diff deletes TestService_getUserPermissions' cache-hit case and adds no test exercising the permDenialCache expiry/grant-recovery behavior — i.e., the new behavior-bearing denial cache's interaction with permission changes and TTL is entirely untested. A regression in denial-cache eviction or in the invalidation gap (finding 1) would pass the full test suite and only surface as users reporting they cannot access newly granted resources in production.

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces new behavior via `permDenialCache` in `Service.Check` (early deny when `permDenialCache.Get(...)` hits, and `permDenialCache.Set(...)` when `!allowed`), but the added tests only cover the presence of an explicit denial entry (`TestService_CacheCheck` "Should deny on explicit cache deny entry") and do not exercise TTL/expiry or "grant-recovery" after permissions change. Additionally, the prior cache-hit unit case in `TestService_getUserPermissions` is removed. This is a specific, diff-grounded test gap for newly added nontrivial caching behavior, not a directly verifiable functional defect from the diff alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The permission-denial cache is populated (line ~153 `s.permDenialCache.Set(ctx, permDenialKey, true)`) but no invalidation path anywhere in this diff deletes denial entries when a user's permissions change, and the denial key format (`namespace + ".perm_" + userUID + "_" + action + "_" + name + "_" + parent`) diverges from the permCache key format (`namespace + ".perm_" + userUID + "_" + action`), so any existing invalidation that targets the permission cache key/prefix pattern does not necessarily match denial entries. A user who is granted access to a resource (e.g. added to a role or given dashboard permissions) keeps receiving Allowed=false for up to shortCacheTTL on every Check, even after the permission cache itself has been invalidated/refreshed — a stale-deny window longer than the permCache staleness, producing access denials that outlive the permission cache's invalidation guarantees.

adjudication.rationale: In `Service.Check`, the new `permDenialCache` is consulted first (`if _, ok := s.permDenialCache.Get(...); ok { return Allowed:false }`) and populated on any deny (`s.permDenialCache.Set(ctx, permDenialKey, true)`). There is no deletion/invalidation of these denial entries shown anywhere in the diff (no `Delete` calls, no coupling to permission refresh), so if permissions in the underlying store later change from deny->allow, `Check` will still return `Allowed=false` until the denial entry expires. This stale-deny behavior is guaranteed by the logic order regardless of whether `permCache` is refreshed, and the denial key format is distinct/more specific than the permCache key, making it unlikely that any permCache-targeted invalidation would clear it.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] When the permission cache HIT yields a denial (allowed==false) and no denial entry exists, Check falls through to `s.metrics.permissionCacheUsage.WithLabelValues("false", checkReq.Action).Inc()` and refetches from the database, recording a cache miss for a request that was actually served from cache and issuing a full DB permission load on every such request. The permissionCacheUsage metric systematically under-reports hit rate for deny outcomes (any cached-perms deny with no prior denial entry is logged as "false" and triggers a redundant getIdentityPermissions DB round-trip), so dashboards monitoring cache effectiveness and DB load on the authz hot path show wrong numbers and the cache provides no benefit for first-time denies.

adjudication.rationale: The diff intentionally treats a cached-permissions denial as non-authoritative and falls back to `getIdentityPermissions` to avoid false negatives from stale/incomplete `permCache` (see new test `Fallback to the database on outdated cache`, where a cache “deny” is expected to be overridden by DB allow). Also, the claim that this causes a DB load “on every such request” is contradicted by the new `permDenialCache`: after a DB-confirmed deny, `Check` stores `permDenialKey` and subsequent requests short-circuit before any DB call. The `permissionCacheUsage` metric being incremented as `"false"` on fallback is consistent with “request served fully from cache” semantics, and the request is not actually served from cache in that path.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The denial-cache lookup and the permission-cache lookup are two parallel caches with overlapping but non-identical key grammars built by string concatenation (userPermCacheKey vs userPermDenialCacheKey in cache.go lines 27-32), where the denial key is the perm key plus `_name_parent` segments — a hand-maintained pair of formats with no shared constructor. The next editor who adds a cache key component (e.g. a folder-path discriminator or identity type) or who writes an invalidation that prefixes on the perm-key pattern will update one format and silently miss the other, producing either denial entries that never match (dead cache) or an invalidation that can't reach denial entries; denials also bypass the folder-tree logic entirely, so a resource moved between folders serves stale denials keyed to the old parent until TTL expiry.

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces a second cache key format `userPermDenialCacheKey(...)` (cache.go) alongside the existing `userPermCacheKey(...)`, built via independent string concatenation. In `Service.Check` the denial cache is checked first using the denial-key grammar, while permission caching uses `userPermCacheKey` via `getCachedIdentityPermissions`. This is a real maintainability/invalidations risk created by the change: future edits that add key components or rely on prefix-based invalidation could easily update one format but not the other, leaving denial entries unreachable or uninvalidateable. However, the diff does not show any invalidation code or a concrete failing behavior (the “stale denial on folder move” claim is not directly verifiable here), so it’s not a demonstrable bug from the patch alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] In List, the cached permissions map returned by getCachedIdentityPermissions (the same map instance stored in the shared permCache) is passed directly to listPermission without any defensive copy, and the same shared-map-by-reference pattern now flows through two read paths (Check via checkPermission and List via listPermission). If listPermission (or any future consumer of the cached map) mutates the map — e.g. adding computed wildcards or normalizing scopes — it corrupts the cached entry for all subsequent requests in the TTL window, turning a shared cache into cross-request state contamination; the exposure is new because this diff adds a second consumer path to the raw cached value.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds `getCachedIdentityPermissions` which returns the cached `map[string]bool` from `s.permCache.Get(...)` directly, and `List` now passes that map straight into `s.listPermission(...)` (and `Check` passes it into `s.checkPermission(...)`). In Go, maps are reference types, so any mutation by `listPermission`/`checkPermission` would mutate the same instance that is stored in the shared cache entry, contaminating subsequent requests within the TTL. However, the diff does not show the implementations of `listPermission` or `checkPermission`, so we cannot verify that they (currently) mutate the map; the finding is a valid, specific risk introduced/exposed by the new cached read path rather than a proven defect from the diff alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The new permDenialCache has no invalidation path, so cached denials persist for shortCacheTTL after a user's permissions are granted, unlike the previous behavior where denials were re-derived from a permCache that existing invalidation code evicts on permission changes. An admin grants a user access to a dashboard they were just denied; the existing permission-change invalidation logic evicts userPermCacheKey entries but knows nothing about userPermDenialCacheKey, so the user keeps getting Allowed:false from the stale denial entry for up to shortCacheTTL, a silent authz-behavior regression relative to the pre-diff contract that invalidation preserved.

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces a new negative-result cache `permDenialCache` that is checked first in `Service.Check` (service.go:113-131) and, on hit, returns `Allowed: false` without re-reading permissions from store/DB. The denial entry is populated whenever `allowed` is false after the DB-backed permission evaluation (service.go:150-153). Within the diff there is no corresponding eviction/invalidation of these `userPermDenialCacheKey(...)` entries (no `Delete` calls anywhere for this cache/key), so after a permission grant the stale denial can persist until `shortCacheTTL` expires, causing a silent authorization regression relative to the new “fallback to DB on outdated cache” behavior added just above.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The denial cache key embeds the request's ParentFolder value verbatim, so the same resource checked with Folder set versus unset produces two independent denial keys and the cached denial leaks into or fails to apply across the two access patterns inconsistently. A Check with ParentFolder="fold1" that is denied populates key ..._dash1_fold1; a subsequent identical request without Folder (ParentFolder="") gets a different key and skips the denial, and a denial recorded for the folder-less key also does not cover folder-inherited access — denial caching becomes path-dependent, which the original always-recomputed Check never was.

adjudication.rationale: The diff does construct the denial cache key using `checkReq.ParentFolder` verbatim (`permDenialKey := userPermDenialCacheKey(..., checkReq.ParentFolder)`), and `userPermDenialCacheKey` appends `"_" + parent` to the key. Therefore, the same `Namespace/UserUID/Action/Name` checked with `ParentFolder="fold1"` vs `ParentFolder=""` will use different denial-cache entries and will not share cached denials. Whether those two requests are semantically equivalent (and thus this is a correctness/security bug) is not provable from the diff alone, but it is a concrete, diff-grounded concern because it can reduce denial-cache effectiveness and make behavior dependent on whether callers populate `Folder`.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] ProvideAuthZClient silently swaps the in-process authz client from a 30s local cache (newRBACClient) to authzlib.NewClient with NoopCache, removing client-side response caching with no flag or config escape hatch. Every in-process authz Check RPC that previously served from the 30s client cache now hits the server each time; operators relying on that cache to blunt burst load on the authz service cannot re-enable it without a code deploy, and the change was not surfaced as a documented behavioral trade-off in the diff.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows `ProvideAuthZClient` switched from `newRBACClient(channel, tracer)` to `authzlib.NewClient(channel, authzlib.WithCacheClientOption(&NoopCache{}), ...)`, and `NoopCache.Get` always returns `cache.ErrNotFound`. This verifiably disables the authzlib client-side cache for the in-process client, whereas the removed `newRBACClient` path used a `cache.NewLocalCache` with a 30s expiry. There is no flag/config in the diff to restore the previous client-cache behavior. While server-side caching was added in `Service.Check/List`, the finding about removing in-process client response caching is accurate and is a behavioral/operational trade-off rather than a clear correctness bug.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] Denial-cache hits are counted under the permissionCacheUsage metric with hit="true", conflating two distinct cache layers into one metric series. Anyone monitoring permissionCacheUsage hit-rate to tune the permission cache TTL will see inflated hit rates from denial entries whose misses never populate the metric path (the hit branch increments but the denial-cache miss is indistinguishable), so cache-tuning dashboards silently change meaning with this diff.

adjudication.rationale: In `Service.Check`, a *denial-cache hit* path increments `s.metrics.permissionCacheUsage.WithLabelValues("true", checkReq.Action).Inc()` and returns `Allowed: false` (see new block starting `permDenialKey := ...` and `if _, ok := s.permDenialCache.Get(...); ok { ... }`). This uses the same `permissionCacheUsage` metric series as permission-cache hits, so observers can’t distinguish “permission cache hit” vs “denial cache hit”. Also, there is no corresponding metric increment for a *denial-cache miss*; misses flow into the later `permissionCacheUsage` "false" increment, making denial-cache behavior indistinguishable from permission-cache misses. This is an observability/metric semantics issue, not a functional defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The new permDenialCache is written on every deny (line ~153) but this diff adds no invalidation path for it, so denials survive permission-cache invalidation events. When a user's permissions change (role granted), existing invalidation logic purges the userPermCache entries, but denial entries keyed as namespace+".perm_"+userUID+"_"+action+"_"+name+"_"+parent (cache.go:30-32) are not registered with any Delete/invalidate call in this diff; a user who was denied once is denied again from the stale denial cache even after the grant, breaking authorization correctness — this is the authorization-cache-asymmetry pattern (grants get fresh DB re-lookup, cached denials are served without revalidation).

adjudication.rationale: In `Service.Check`, the new `permDenialCache` is consulted first and returns an immediate deny if the key exists (`if _, ok := s.permDenialCache.Get(...); ok { return Allowed:false }`). On any DB-evaluated deny, the code writes `s.permDenialCache.Set(..., true)` and there is no corresponding delete/clear path shown (no `Delete` call, and no logic to remove/override a prior denial when the user later becomes allowed). Because the denial check happens before any cached-permission or DB revalidation, a stale denial entry will continue to deny requests until TTL/explicit invalidation, which is authorization-incorrect if permissions change during that window.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] userPermDenialCacheKey embeds the raw request-supplied Name and ParentFolder, producing an unbounded per-resource key space that no exact-key invalidation can cover. Operators performing cache invalidation on permission change cannot enumerate the (action, name, parent) combinations previously denied for a user, so any invalidation strategy short of deleting by prefix will leave stale denial entries; whoever wires up invalidation next must know about this second key family or the deny cache silently diverges from the grant cache.

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces a new negative-permission cache keyed by `userPermDenialCacheKey(namespace, userUID, action, name, parent)` (see `pkg/services/authz/rbac/cache.go`) and used in `Service.Check` to short-circuit denies. That key embeds request-specific `Name` and `ParentFolder` (`permDenialKey := ... checkReq.Name, checkReq.ParentFolder`), creating a potentially unbounded per-resource key space distinct from the existing grant cache (`userPermCacheKey` only depends on user+action). While this is not a directly verifiable functional defect in this diff (no invalidation mechanism is shown), it is a concrete, diff-grounded maintainability/operability concern: any future invalidation that only targets the existing permission cache keys would not clear these denial entries, and enumerating all (name,parent) combinations is impractical without prefix deletion.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] A denied Check is written to permDenialCache with no invalidation in this diff, so a permission granted within shortCacheTTL is still denied, and the new TestService_CacheCheck only asserts the deny-on-hit path — it never tests a subsequent grant after a cached denial, leaving the stale-denial window completely unverified. A user who has a dashboard shared to them within ~30s of a denied Check keeps getting Allowed=false from the denial cache even though the permission store and permCache now say allowed; no test in the diff exercises grant-after-deny, so a regression or TTL increase here ships silently.

adjudication.rationale: In `Service.Check`, the new `permDenialCache` is consulted first and, on a hit, immediately returns `Allowed: false` without checking `permCache` or re-fetching from the store (`if _, ok := s.permDenialCache.Get(...); ok { ... return &authzv1.CheckResponse{Allowed: false}, nil }`). Later, on any computed denial, the code writes `s.permDenialCache.Set(ctx, permDenialKey, true)` with only TTL-based expiry and no invalidation/override logic. This means a previously denied (namespace,user,action,name,parentFolder) can remain denied for `shortCacheTTL` even if permissions for that object become allowed and `permCache`/store would now permit it, because the deny cache short-circuits all other checks. The added tests include a deny-on-hit case but do not exercise the grant-after-deny scenario, so this stale-denial behavior is unverified in the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The new getCachedIdentityPermissions switch branches for types.TypeAnonymous (cache hit), types.TypeRenderService (always miss), and the default error path are exercised by no test in the diff — TestService_CacheCheck and TestService_CacheList only cover TypeUser via 'user:test-uid' subjects, and no other test file in the diff (only pkg/services/authz/rbac/service_test.go changed) calls Check or List with an anonymous or render-service subject. A regression in the anonymous cached-permission path (e.g. wrong cache key or returning stale perms) or the default-case error handling would not be caught by any test; anonymous traffic through the authz service is a major request path.

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces new nontrivial branching logic in `getCachedIdentityPermissions(...)` (new in `pkg/services/authz/rbac/service.go`) with explicit cases for `types.TypeAnonymous` (uses `anonymousPermCacheKey` and `s.permCache.Get`), `types.TypeRenderService` (always returns `cache.ErrNotFound`), and a `default` that returns an error for unsupported identity types. The newly added tests `TestService_CacheCheck` and `TestService_CacheList` in `pkg/services/authz/rbac/service_test.go` only exercise the user path by passing subjects like `"user:test-uid"`, and nothing in the shown diff adds tests that call `Check`/`List` with an anonymous or render-service identity or that forces the default error path. This is a specific, diff-grounded test gap for newly added logic rather than a demonstrated functional defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The new cached-branch error path in Check (checkPermission failing on cachedPerms) increments requestCount with the 'true' cache-usage label combination but the tests never trigger it, and no test asserts any metrics label values for the new denial/cached paths at all — the new tests assert only resp.Allowed. If the label wiring for the new cache paths is wrong (the deny path labels requestCount 'false' while permissionCacheUsage is 'true'), dashboards built on permissionCacheUsage will misreport hit rates, and no test will notice because metrics are never asserted in TestService_CacheCheck/CacheList.

adjudication.rationale: In `Service.Check`, a new cached-permissions fast path was added: it calls `getCachedIdentityPermissions` and then `checkPermission` (and on error increments `s.metrics.requestCount.WithLabelValues("true", "true", ...)` before returning). The newly added tests (`TestService_CacheCheck` / `TestService_CacheList`) only assert `resp.Allowed` / listed items and never assert any metric label values, and none of them trigger the cached-branch `checkPermission` error path. So regressions in the new cache-path metrics wiring (or mislabeling between `permissionCacheUsage` vs `requestCount`) would not be caught by tests. This is a concrete test coverage/observability gap introduced by the diff, but not a proven functional bug.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The new permDenialCache is written on every denied Check but has no invalidation path anywhere in this diff, so a permission grant does not clear previously cached denials. When an admin grants a user access to a dashboard (the permission-updated path invalidates permCache/idCache but never touches permDenialCache), the user keeps receiving Allowed:false from the denial entry for up to shortCacheTTL after the grant, breaking the previously-immediate effect of permission changes; the same staleness applies when a resource is moved into a folder the user can read.

adjudication.rationale: In `Service.Check`, a denial is cached unconditionally (`if !allowed { s.permDenialCache.Set(...) }`) and future checks short-circuit to `Allowed:false` solely on the presence of that key (`if _, ok := s.permDenialCache.Get(...); ok { return Allowed:false }`). Within this diff there is no corresponding `Delete`/invalidation of `permDenialCache` anywhere, so once a deny is cached it can override later permission changes for up to `shortCacheTTL`, causing incorrect denials relative to the current permission store.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] Check caches a denial (permDenialCache.Set) even when the deny decision was computed from a stale permCache hit path falling through to the database, and it stores the denial keyed on the raw request's Name/ParentFolder without ensuring ParentFolder was resolved. A request whose ParentFolder field is empty (or resolved later inside checkPermission against the folder tree) writes a denial under key suffix '_<empty>' that is never matched by later requests carrying an explicit folder, and vice versa, so denials are cached under inconsistent keys; more importantly, any transient deny (e.g., mid-deploy skew, folder tree still cold) is pinned for the full TTL with no way to purge it.

adjudication.rationale: The diff does introduce a new negative cache in `Service.Check` keyed as `userPermDenialCacheKey(ns, userUID, action, name, parentFolder)` using `checkReq.ParentFolder` directly (see added block at the start of `Check` and `userPermDenialCacheKey` in `cache.go`). This means a denial cached when `ParentFolder` is empty will not be reused when later requests include a non-empty folder (and vice versa), which can make the denial cache ineffective/inconsistent across request shapes. However, the finding’s stronger claim that the denial is cached based on a “stale permCache hit path” is not supported: the code only calls `permDenialCache.Set(...)` after computing `allowed` from the fresh `permissions` returned by `getIdentityPermissions(...)` (DB path), not from the cached-permissions path. The “transient deny pinned for TTL” is more of a design/performance/behavior concern inherent to negative caching, not a clearly verifiable correctness defect from the diff alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] On a permDenialCache hit, Check returns Allowed:false without ever validating that the subject's identifiers or permissions were loadable, so a deny caused by a transient backend error path that reached the Set at line ~153 is replayed as an authoritative deny. The Set at the bottom of Check runs unconditionally whenever !allowed, including denies that stem from degraded store reads surfaced through getIdentityPermissions' non-error deny results; users whose check was denied during a partial backend failure stay locked out of that exact resource for the full TTL with no re-evaluation, whereas pre-diff behavior re-queried the store on every request.

adjudication.rationale: The diff does introduce a negative-cache short-circuit: in `Service.Check`, a `permDenialCache` hit immediately returns `Allowed:false` before loading identifiers or permissions (`if _, ok := s.permDenialCache.Get(...); ok { ... return &CheckResponse{Allowed:false} }`). Also, the code unconditionally populates this cache for any computed `!allowed` result (`s.permDenialCache.Set(...)`). However, the finding’s framing around a “transient backend error path” is not verifiable from the diff: when `getIdentityPermissions` returns an error, `Check` returns early and does not set the denial cache. The risk of caching a deny derived from incomplete/non-error store results is speculative given only this diff, making it a design/edge-case concern rather than a clearly provable defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The new permDenialCache is written on every DB-backed denial but has no invalidation path anywhere in the diff, so a cached denial survives permission grants. A user denied once is denied for the full shortCacheTTL (30s) even after an admin grants the permission and any permission-change invalidation fires — permCache gets invalidated on writes but permDenialCache is a new key family no existing invalidation code knows about, so the grant silently fails to take effect until TTL expiry; the denial-cache-hit branch returns Allowed:false without ever consulting fresh state.

adjudication.rationale: In Service.Check, a permDenialCache entry is consulted first and returns Allowed:false immediately if present (service.go:113-132). The cache is written on any DB-backed denial (service.go:150-154) but there is no code in this diff that ever deletes/invalidates these denial keys or clears them when a later check would be allowed. Therefore, once a denial is cached for (namespace,user,action,name,parent), subsequent checks will be denied until TTL expiry even if underlying permissions change or permCache is refreshed, because the denial short-circuits before consulting cachedPerms/DB.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] A permDenialCache hit is recorded as permissionCacheUsage("true") and requestCount(cache_hit="true") even though the permission cache itself was never consulted, corrupting cache-hit dashboards. Operators tuning cache effectiveness see inflated permission-cache hit rates driven by denial entries, and cannot distinguish denial-cache hits from permission-cache hits when debugging authz latency/staleness; the metric content misdirects the investigation.

adjudication.rationale: In Service.Check, a permDenialCache hit short-circuits before consulting permCache (it returns immediately after `s.permDenialCache.Get(...)` succeeds), yet it increments `s.metrics.permissionCacheUsage.WithLabelValues("true", checkReq.Action)` and `s.metrics.requestCount.WithLabelValues("false", "true", ...)` in that branch. This makes denial-cache hits indistinguishable from permission-cache hits in these metrics, inflating/contaminating cache-hit dashboards. The diff shows this metrics labeling behavior, but it does not affect authorization correctness (it still returns `Allowed: false`).

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] Non-ErrNotFound errors from getCachedIdentityPermissions (e.g. a store failure from GetUserIdentifiers for TypeUser) are silently discarded with no log and the code falls through to getIdentityPermissions, which re-issues the same identifier query. When the identifier store is failing, every Check pays a doubled, unlogged round trip to the failing store before the error is finally surfaced by getIdentityPermissions, and the transient failure is invisible in logs because only the final error is recorded.

adjudication.rationale: In `Service.Check`, the result of `getCachedIdentityPermissions(...)` is only used when `err == nil`; any non-nil error is silently ignored and execution falls through to `getIdentityPermissions(...)` (see the new block starting `cachedPerms, err := ...` and the subsequent unconditional call to `s.getIdentityPermissions`). In `getCachedIdentityPermissions`, the `TypeUser`/`TypeServiceAccount` path calls `s.GetUserIdentifiers(...)` and returns its error directly. Therefore, if the identifier lookup fails (non-`cache.ErrNotFound`), `Check` will discard that error without logging and then call `getIdentityPermissions`, which will re-issue the identifier lookup again, causing duplicated failing calls and delayed/less clear observability. This is a concrete, diff-grounded efficiency/telemetry issue rather than a functional correctness defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] When cached permissions are found but evaluate to allowed==false, permissionCacheUsage is incremented with "false" (cache miss) even though the cache was a hit, and the code then re-fetches from the store and overwrites the denial cache entry. Dashboards under-report permission-cache effectiveness because denies via cached data are counted as misses, and operators measuring cache benefit from these metrics get a systematically wrong picture of the Check fast path.
matched_golden_ids: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: The candidate flags that cached denials (allowed==false) are treated as misses: the code re-fetches from the store and overwrites the denial cache entry. This describes the same asymmetric cache-trust behavior as the golden issue (trust cached grants but ignore cached denials). While the candidate emphasizes metric/reporting impact rather than the security risk from stale grants, it identifies the same underlying logic flaw.
